extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students of poetics/theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and evaluating tragic drama: how to construct plot, characters, diction, and theatrical elements so a tragedy arouses pity and fear and forms a coherent artistic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ... must represent one action, a complete whole, with its several incidents so closely connected that the transposal or withdrawal of any one of them will disjoin and dislocate the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a single, coherent action as the subject; remove or add nothing that does not make a perceptible difference to the whole. Example: Homer chose one action for the Odyssey rather than attempting to narrate every event in the hero's life. Anti-pattern: episodic sequences whose episodes lack probable or necessary connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet represents universals (probable or necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet’s function is to describe not the thing that has happened, but a kind of thing that might happen, i.e. what is possible as being probable or necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for universality—portray what such a kind of person would probably or necessarily say or do, rather than merely recounting singular historical facts. This makes poetry more 'philosophic' than history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Of simple plots and actions the episodic are the worst. I call a plot episodic when there is neither probability nor necessity in the sequence of its episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assemble loosely connected episodes; episodes should be appropriate and functionally tied to the central action. Episodes may be used to lengthen epic works, but in drama they must be short and integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must arouse pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ... is an imitation not only of a complete action, but also of incidents arousing pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose incidents that naturally evoke pity and fear—preferably those that occur unexpectedly yet as a consequence of one another. This is the proper pleasure of tragedy; aim to produce these emotions primarily through plot, not spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marvel and appearance of design (chance with seeming purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even matters of chance seem most marvellous if there is an appearance of design as it were in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If chance events are used, shape them so they appear meaningful or designed by the plot's structure, which makes them satisfying rather than arbitrary (example: the statue of Mitys incident).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs complex plot distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple action ... I call simple when the change in the hero’s fortunes takes place without peripety or discovery; and complex, when it involves one or the other, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (discovery) should be present; if present, they must arise naturally from antecedent events rather than being tacked on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripety (reversal) and its proper function
rubrics_metrics.description: A peripety is the change from one state of things within the play to its opposite ... in the probable or necessary sequence of events; as it is for instance in Oedipus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft reversals so that they follow necessarily or probably from prior events in the plot, thereby intensifying tragic effect. They should not feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery (anagnorisis) and its proper form
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery is ... a change from ignorance to knowledge, and thus to either love or hate in the personages marked for good or evil fortune. The finest form of discovery is one attended by peripeties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor discoveries rooted in the plot's incidents (best) rather than contrived signs or poet's narration; combine discovery with reversal when possible (example: Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering as a constituent element
rubrics_metrics.description: A third part is suffering, which we may define as an action of a destructive or painful nature, such as murders on the stage, tortures, woundings, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use suffering where it serves the plot's emotional aims; suffering is a distinct formative element alongside peripety and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural parts of tragedy (by quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the point of view of its quantity ... a tragedy has the following parts: prologue, episode, exode, and a choral portion, distinguished into parode and stasimon; ... songs from the stage and commoe are only found in some.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the play into these functional sections: prologue (before first choral entry), episodes (between choruses), exode (after last chorus), parode (first chorus statement), stasimon (choral song without anapaests/trochees), commos (chorus+actor lament).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plots to avoid (character/outcome constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three forms of plot to be avoided. (1) A good man must not be seen passing from happiness to misery; (2) a bad man from misery to happiness; (3) an extremely bad man be seen falling from happiness into misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots that are odious, untragic, or unmovingly unjust. The ideal tragic protagonist is intermediate—neither preeminent in virtue nor vicious—but falls from happiness to misery through some great error of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic plot and protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfect plot ... must have a single ... issue; the change in the hero’s fortunes must be ... from happiness to misery; and the cause of it must lie not in any depravity, but in some great error on his part; the man himself being ... not worse than he was before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a single, unified outcome (not double issue). Make the protagonist relatable (a man like ourselves) whose downfall comes from error (hamartia), not vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should be effective as narration (not rely on spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot in fact should be so framed that, even without seeing the things take place, he who simply hears the account of them shall be filled with horror and pity at the incidents; ... To produce this same effect by means of the spectacle is less artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents so that recital alone conveys their tragic power. Excess reliance on spectacle (mere monstrous spectacle) is inferior art and may betray poor plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer familial settings for tragic deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the tragic deed ... is done within the family, when murder or the like is done or meditated by brother on brother, by son on father, by mother on son, or son on mother, these are the situations the poet should seek after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use close personal/blood relationships to heighten pity and horror (examples: Clytaemnestra/Orestes, Eriphyle/Alcmeon). Traditional myths often supply such material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes and ranking of the deed (knowing/ignorant/recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deed of horror may be done by the doer knowingly ... Or he may do it, but in ignorance of his relationship, and discover that afterwards ... A third possibility is for one meditating some deadly injury ... to make the discovery in time to draw back. The worst situation is when ... with full knowledge ... and leaves it undone. ... Next after this comes the actual perpetration ... A better situation than that, however, is for the deed to be done in ignorance, and the relationship discovered afterwards, ... But the best of all is the last; ... where recognition in time prevents the deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank dramatic configurations: worst—intent without act (odious); better—act done knowingly; better still—act done in ignorance discovered later; best—recognition in time to prevent the deed (examples: Cresphontes, Iphigenia). Use these permutations deliberately for emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character construction: four aims
rubrics_metrics.description: In the characters there are four points to aim at. First and foremost, that they shall be good. ... The second point is to make them appropriate. ... The third is to make them like the reality. The fourth is to make them consistent and the same throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters who (1) reveal morally good purpose where needed, (2) are appropriate to role/gender/status, (3) resemble real human types, and (4) are consistent (even if 'consistently inconsistent'). Avoid gratuitous baseness, incongruity, or inconsistent transfigurations (examples: Menelaus in Orestes; Iphigenia at Aulis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery (anagnorisis) species and hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Species of discovery: (1) by signs or marks (least artistic), (2) made directly by the poet (inartistic), (3) by memory, (4) by reasoning, (5) composite discovery from bad reasoning, (6) best—arising from the incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer discoveries that emerge naturally from incidents (most artistic). Avoid obvious token-based or poet-inserted revelations; use memory and reasoning appropriately. Examples: Ulysses’ scar (signs), Orestes revealed by a letter (memory), Oedipus (incidents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's craft during composition (visualization, enactment, simplification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should remember (1) to put the actual scenes as far as possible before his eyes; (2) as far as may be, the poet should even act his story with the very gestures of his personages; (3) his story ... he should first simplify and reduce to a universal form, before proceeding to lengthen it out by the insertion of episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work from vivid visualization and physical sense of scenes; rehearse or act gestures to capture emotions truthfully; reduce to a tight universal plot before adding episodes, and ensure episodes are appropriate to the core action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and dénouement mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy is in part complication and in part dénouement; the incidents before the opening scene ... forming the complication; and the rest the dénouement. ... It is right ... to speak of a tragedy as the same or not the same as another, on the ground ... of their plot, i.e. complication and dénouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly delineate complication (all up to the change in hero's fortunes) and dénouement (from change to end). Ensure both are well constructed—many dramatists succeed in complication but fail in dénouement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four species of tragedy and element combination
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four distinct species of tragedy ...: first, the complex tragedy (peripety and discovery); second, the tragedy of suffering; third, the tragedy of character; fourth, that of spectacle. The poet’s aim, then, should be to combine every element of interest, if possible, or else the more important and the major part of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand which species your work most closely aligns with and strive to combine major elements (plot, character, thought, diction, melody, spectacle) appropriately. Beware critics expecting a single poet to surpass predecessors in every species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus too should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole, and take a share in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write choral parts that participate in or advance the plot (Sophoclean model) rather than intercalary songs unrelated to the action (a later decline observed in some poets). Treat chorus as a component of dramatic causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dramatizing an entire epic (scale mismatch)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should also remember ... and not write a tragedy on an epic body of incident (i.e. one with a plurality of stories in it), by attempting to dramatize, for instance, the entire story of the Iliad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to compress an epic-scale plurality of stories into a single drama; such scale mismatches usually fail on stage. Instead select a coherent portion suitable to tragic unity (Euripides/Aeschylus strategies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (theme) and diction: clarity and nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of diction is for it to be at once clear and not mean. The clearest indeed is that made up of the ordinary words for things; but it is mean. ... A certain admixture of unfamiliar terms is necessary. ... The greatest thing by far is to be a master of metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for diction that is both clear and elevated: combine ordinary words (for clarity) with strange words, metaphors, ornamental forms (for distinction), but practice moderation. Metaphor mastery is a sign of genius; use figurative language judiciously as genre-appropriate (compounds in dithyramb, strange words in heroic, metaphor in iambic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and uses of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor consists in giving the thing a name that belongs to something else ... from genus to species, from species to genus, from species to species, or on grounds of analogy. ... There is also ... qualified metaphor ... and coined words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ different metaphor types (genus↔species, species↔species, analogy) to create striking images; qualify metaphors when helpful. Use coined or altered words sparingly and only where they enhance non-prosaic quality without becoming riddles or barbarisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in poetic license (strange words, compounds, forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A too apparent use of these licences has certainly a ludicrous effect, but they are not alone in that; the rule of moderation applies to all the constituents of the poetic vocabulary ... The mere fact of their not being in ordinary speech gives the diction a non-prosaic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance novelty with intelligibility: excessive unfamiliarity produces riddles or barbarisms; ordinary words alone produce meanness. Test lines by substituting normal words to judge effect.
